newsitem.title: FRANCE: Grim mood at last pre-poll French cabinet meeting.
newsitem.headline: Grim mood at last pre-poll French cabinet meeting.

text.p: The looks on many of their faces and the bitterness in some of their voices said it all: France's outgoing cabinet ministers are haunted by a possible defeat at the polls.

If the mood in the courtyard of the Elysee presidential palace after the last meeting of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's outgoing cabinet was any measure, the centre-right coalition seems set to lose Sunday's parliamentary election runoff.

"We don't intend to leave France to those who want to take it back to the past," said an angry Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, among those most upset by last Sunday's surprise left-wing surge in the first round of voting.

"France cannot change direction at each election. You can't swing 180 degrees and go off a different way each time you vote. We'd be the only people in the world to do this," Education Minister Francois Bayrou added.
Both men said they would fight to the last. But others spoke as if President Jacques Chirac's nightmare -- "cohabitation" with a left-wing cabinet -- had already come true.

"I've experienced some intense moments in stadiums in my life," said Sports Minister Guy Drut, the 1976 Olympic Games gold medal hurdler. "Well, now I've lived through two nice years in a cabinet that did good work but clearly wasn't popular."
The tall, smiling Drut, who seems sure of retaining his own parliamentary seat, sounded philosophical, as befits a veteran athlete who has known both disappointment and victory.
But Junior Minister for Integration Eric Raoult looked more emotional. "The others may get back in but, as for myself, I don't know," he said.

Raoult faces defeat in his constituency, meaning that in a space of two weeks, he could go from occupying a ministerial post with chauffered limousines to being mayor of a blue collar Paris suburb that no longer wants him as its man in parliament.
Officials on President Chirac's staff, whose own jobs are secure, were cautious about predicting Sunday's outcome. "We can always hope that the French will wake up in time," one said.

The often intense Juppe, apparently reconciled to a period in the political wilderness, showed a glimpse of wry humour when he came out of the Elysee palace only to be trapped in a melee of reporters trying to record the last words of his term.

As bodyguards shoved their elbows into journalists' ribs to clear a path for Juppe, the prime minister turned to one burly guard and said: "You don't have to protect me. I don't think these (the journalists) are the ones who have it in for me."
